name: Mughal Empire
line: Be at peace with all, look closely at the world and make something beautiful of the day.

quote.text: It is my duty to be in good understanding with all men. If they walk in the way of God’s will, interference with them would be in itself reprehensible; and if otherwise, they are under the malady of ignorance and deserve my compassion.
quote.source: Letter to Shah Abbas of Persia, 1594, in Abu’l-Fazl, Akbarnama, trans. H. Beveridge

quotes.text: I have simply written the truth. I do not intend by what I have written to compliment myself; I have simply set down exactly what happened.
quotes.source: The Baburnama, his memoirs, about 1529, trans. Wheeler M. Thackston

quotes.text: If there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this.
quotes.by: Persian couplet attributed to Amir Khusrau
quotes.source: Inscribed in gold on the walls of the Hall of Private Audience in the Red Fort, Delhi, 1648

quotes.text: Jesus, son of Mary, on whom be peace, said: The world is a bridge. Pass over it, but build no houses upon it.
quotes.source: On the Buland Darwaza, Akbar’s great gateway at Fatehpur Sikri, 1601

quotes.text: Let nothing cover my grave save the green grass, for grass suffices as the covering of the lowly.
quotes.source: The Persian verse she composed for her own open-topped tomb at the shrine of Nizamuddin, Delhi, 1681

quotes.text: Thousands of desires, each one worth dying for. Many of my wishes were fulfilled, and yet they were few.
quotes.source: The opening couplet of a ghazal, Delhi, about 1850. Translated from the Urdu

quotes.text: One teardrop on the cheek of time.
quotes.source: On the Taj Mahal, from his Bengali poem Shah Jahan, 1914

words.usage: Akbar’s governing principle: the ruler favours no religion over another, and every subject is under his protection.
The title Babur took at Kabul in 1507. It means master king.
The formal assembly at which the emperor heard petitions, received envoys and gave orders, with everyone standing in order of rank.
Each sunrise the emperor showed himself at a window in the palace wall so that the people could see he was alive and bring him their complaints.
A pillared hall open on three sides, where anyone might in principle approach the throne.
The inner hall for ministers, ambassadors and confidential business.
A number, from ten to several thousand, that fixed a noble’s pay and the cavalry he must maintain. Persians, Turks, Afghans, Rajputs and Indian Muslims all held them.
An order under the emperor’s seal, written in a fine hand and often beautifully illuminated.
A walled world of several thousand women with its own officers, incomes and politics. Senior women traded, built and advised.
A walled garden divided by water channels into four, recalling the rivers of paradise. Babur brought the form to India.
Mughal rulers camped, held court, celebrated and were buried in gardens.
The hall at Fatehpur Sikri where Akbar gathered scholars of every religion to debate before him on Thursday nights.
The whole code of courteous conduct: how to greet, sit, speak, eat and disagree. Also a word of greeting.
Polished manners and taste. The shared culture of Hindus and Muslims in the northern cities is called the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb, after the two rivers that meet.
Placing the back of the right hand on the ground and raising it gently to the head while standing up.
A garment, ideally one the emperor had worn, given as a mark of favour. To put it on was to accept his service.
Gold coins offered on a cloth when approaching the emperor. He touched them and often gave more in return.
The imperial library and workshop, where calligraphers, painters, gilders and binders worked together on manuscripts.
Court painters signed with humble phrases. Jahangir boasted he could tell which of them had painted each face in a picture.
Flowers of cut carnelian, jade and lapis set flush into white marble. The decoration of the Taj Mahal.
A lattice carved from a single slab, which lets in air and patterned light and keeps out glare and eyes.
Scent distilled from flowers into sandalwood oil. Jahangir records that Nur Jahan’s mother discovered the attar of roses.

words.meaning: A gathering for music or poetry
words.usage: An intimate evening in which the listeners’ appreciation is part of the performance.
Poets recite in turn, a candle is placed before each, and the audience answers good lines aloud.
Each couplet is complete in itself, and all share a rhyme and refrain. Its subject is love, human or divine, usually unattained.
Two lines that must hold a whole thought. People quote them in conversation as proof and as comfort.
A set of notes and phrases with a mood, a season and an hour of the day. The court musician Tansen is credited with several.

words.meaning: The spread cloth for a meal
words.usage: The cloth on the floor around which diners sit, and by extension the whole art of the table.

words.meaning: Betel leaf folded round areca nut and spices
words.usage: Offered at the end of a meal or an audience. To be given it by the emperor’s hand was an honour.
A favourite Mughal word. Jahangir’s full title was Light of the Faith, and he named his wife Nur Jahan, Light of the World.

practices.name: Appear at sunrise
practices.instructions: Be up before the sun and go to a window, a balcony or your doorstep. Watch the sun rise and greet it in silence. Then make yourself available. Ask each person in your household, or message the people who depend on you, what they need today. Listen to one complaint without defending yourself. The rule of this Onda is to be seen, and to hear complaints.
practices.why: The Mughal emperors showed themselves each morning at the jharokha, a balcony window, so that all could see them and bring petitions. Being available is the root of good leadership.
variations: Greet the sun and then your neighbours.
Ask a family member what they need.
Answer a petition you have been avoiding.

practices.name: Write exactly what happened
practices.instructions: Write one page in a notebook as Babur did: plainly, exactly and without flattering yourself. Describe one thing from the natural world that you have looked at closely today, a tree, a fruit, a bird, the weather, with its size, colour and habits. Then describe one thing you did, including a fault. The rule of this Onda is to write the truth about yourself.
practices.why: The Baburnama, written by the first Mughal emperor, is among the first honest autobiographies, with sharp observation of nature and unflinching self-description.
variations: Describe a fruit as Babur would.
Admit one fault.
Write about a place you passed.

practices.name: Draw it exactly
practices.instructions: Draw one plant, bird or animal from life, as closely as you can, in the manner of Ustad Mansur, the court painter of Jahangir. Look at the real thing, not a photograph. Notice the shape of each feather or leaf, its colour and pattern. Add a note: name, place and date. Take your time, and draw what you see, not what you know.
practices.why: Mansur’s natural history paintings of birds, flowers and animals are among the most accurate ever made. Drawing from life trains the eye like nothing else.
variations: Draw a leaf with all its veins.
Draw a bird at the window.
Draw a fruit and then eat it.

practices.name: A scent for the day
practices.instructions: Choose a scent for the day: a drop of attar, rosewater, sandalwood oil, a clove or a sprig of mint. Put a small amount on your wrist or a handkerchief. Mughal courtiers perfumed themselves and their rooms with great care, and Nur Jahan is credited with the discovery of rose attar. Smell it at midday and enjoy it.
practices.why: Fragrance was an essential part of Mughal refinement. A single scent worn with care is a daily luxury.
variations: Scent a handkerchief and give it away.
Burn a stick of incense safely.
Rub a leaf of mint in your hands.

practices.name: A courteous greeting
practices.instructions: Greet each person you meet today with adab, courtesy: a slight bow, a hand brought to the forehead, or a warm word such as adab arz hai. Use their title, ask after their family and take your leave politely. Keep good manners is a rule of this Onda. Notice how a formal greeting softens a day.
practices.why: Adab, etiquette and refinement, was the foundation of the Mughal court and of the tehzeeb of North India. Good manners are a gift to everyone.
variations: Greet an elder with a salaam.
Bow slightly when you thank someone.
Learn a courteous phrase in Urdu.

practices.name: Wish peace to all
practices.instructions: Before you start the day, name one person you disagree with, one of another faith or view, and one stranger, and wish each peace. Say it silently: may you be at peace. Akbar’s principle of sulh-i kull, peace with all, was the heart of his policy. Let it be the day’s first thought.
practices.why: Sulh-i kull, universal peace, was Akbar’s ideal of tolerance and respect for all faiths. A morning wish is a practical way to put it into effect.
variations: Say it for three people.
Write it on a card.
Include someone you find difficult.

practices.name: The house of dialogue
practices.instructions: Give twenty minutes to a view of the world that is not yours. Read a page of another tradition’s scripture, or sit with someone of a different religion, politics or background and ask them to explain what they hold most dear. Don’t argue. Ask for the best form of their belief. Akbar held these debates in his Ibadat Khana every Thursday evening. The rule of this Onda is to be at peace with all.
practices.why: Akbar’s House of Worship hosted Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians, Christians and others in open debate. A modest version at home builds understanding.
variations: Read from another scripture.
Ask a neighbour about their festival.
Visit a place of worship as a guest.

practices.name: The fourfold garden
practices.instructions: Spend twenty minutes in a garden near the end of the day. If you have any ground or even a tray of pots, arrange it in four parts round a centre, and tend it: water, weed, tie up, plant something scented. If you have none, sit in a park and notice its layout. Babur made charbagh, four-part gardens, wherever he went, even in Hindustan, which he found dull. The rule of this Onda is to make beauty part of use.
practices.why: The charbagh, a garden quartered by channels of water, is the Mughal ideal of paradise on earth. From Kabul to Agra, Babur and his heirs built them everywhere.
variations: Plant a scented herb.
Water the plants at dusk.
Sit by a fountain or water bowl.

practices.name: Cut a paper lattice
practices.instructions: Make a jali, a pierced lattice screen of the kind seen in Mughal tombs and palaces. Fold a sheet of paper in half and half again, draw a simple geometric shape on it, and cut it out with scissors or a craft knife. Unfold it and hold it to the light. The patterns of light and shadow are the whole point. Cut away from your fingers.
practices.why: Jali screens of carved stone filter light and air at the Taj Mahal and Fatehpur Sikri. A paper version is a cheap and beautiful craft.
variations: Make a star or flower pattern.
Hang it at a window.
Cut a whole row.

practices.name: A game of ganjifa or chaupar
practices.instructions: Play a game from the Mughal court. Chaupar, the cross-shaped race game, was played by Akbar with living slave-girls as pieces in a courtyard; use cowries or dice and a cloth board. Ganjifa, the round painted card game, can be mimicked with any deck. Play with a friend, laugh and let the dice decide.
practices.why: Chaupar and ganjifa were passions of the Mughal court. Both are easy to play and quick to learn.
variations: Make a chaupar board from cloth.
Play a round of ganjifa online.
Teach a child the game.

practices.name: Look into a miniature
practices.instructions: Look at a Mughal miniature painting online or in a book for fifteen minutes: a court scene, a hunt, a garden. Start at the centre, then move to the corners. Find the smallest detail: a bird, a flower, a face in the crowd. Notice the colour and the lines. Tell yourself the story of the picture.
practices.why: Mughal miniatures combine Persian, Indian and European ideas with extraordinary detail. Looking slowly is the way to enjoy them.
variations: Look at the Padshahnama.
Look at Mansur’s birds.
Draw a detail.

practices.name: A gift of respect
practices.instructions: Offer a small gift to someone you respect, in the manner of a nazr, a ceremonial offering to a superior. Choose something modest but fine: fruit, a flower, a book, a jar of preserves. Present it with both hands and a word of thanks for what they have given you. Receive such a gift graciously when it is offered to you.
practices.why: Gifts were an essential part of Mughal court life, exchanged at every audience. A small, thoughtful offering honours a relationship.
variations: Give fruit to a teacher.
Send flowers to an elder.
Give a book to a friend.

practices.name: An evening of verse and raga
practices.instructions: Close the day with a small mehfil. Sit on the floor with cushions, a lamp and something to drink. Listen to one raga meant for the evening, such as Yaman, for fifteen minutes with your eyes closed. Then read two or three couplets of Urdu or Persian poetry aloud, taking turns if you are with others. Say wah, wah, after a line you love. The rule of this Onda is to make beauty part of the day.
practices.why: The mehfil was the Mughal gathering of music and poetry, held in the evening. It lives on in the ghazal nights of North India and Pakistan.
variations: Read Ghalib in translation.
Light a lamp in the centre.
Have each guest bring a couplet.

practices.name: A night of ghazals
practices.instructions: Play a ghazal by Begum Akhtar or another great singer, a lyric poem of love and loss, sung to a slow beat. Follow a translation of one verse. Lean back and let the singer stretch each line. The Mughal court and later Delhi were the birthplace of the Urdu ghazal, with Ghalib as its master.
practices.why: The ghazal, a poem of rhyming couplets, reached its peak in Mughal Delhi. Begum Akhtar’s voice is the classic of its singing.
variations: Listen with a cup of tea.
Read the lyrics in translation.
Clap along on the beat.

practices.name: Supper on a cloth
practices.instructions: Spread a cloth on the floor, a dastarkhwan, and eat the evening meal on it in the Mughal manner: wash hands first, sit crossways on cushions and share dishes from the middle. Put out rice, a stew, bread, yoghurt and fruit. Serve guests and elders first. End with a sweet and a cup of tea. Good manners at table are a pleasure.
practices.why: The dastarkhwan, a cloth laid on the floor, was the dining table of the Mughal court. Sharing from common dishes encourages conversation.
variations: Use brass or copper dishes.
Wash up together.
Invite an elder and honour them.

practices.name: Lights through a lattice
practices.instructions: Light a few small lamps or candles behind a pierced screen, a colander, a perforated tin or a paper jali, and watch the light spread as stars on the wall. Turn off other lights. The Mughals loved the play of light through jali. Sit and watch the patterns move. Never leave candles unattended.
practices.why: The effect of light through stone lattices is among the glories of Mughal architecture. A simple version at home is magical.
variations: Use a pierced tin can.
Use coloured glass.
Do it in a dark room with incense.

practices.name: Akbar and Birbal
practices.instructions: Tell a story of Akbar and his wise minister Birbal to someone, for example the one where Birbal is told to draw a line shorter without erasing it and draws a longer one beside it. Tell it with a twinkle. These tales are told to children in India and Pakistan. Ask the listener what clever answer they would give.
practices.why: The tales of Akbar and Birbal are famous throughout South Asia, full of wit and good sense. Telling them is a bedtime pleasure.
variations: Tell one to a child.
Look up three more.
Make up a new riddle.

practices.name: Write a sher
practices.instructions: Write a sher, a two-line couplet in the manner of Urdu poetry, about love, the evening or the passing of time. Each line must stand alone yet complete the sense with the other. Try a rhyme at the end. Read it aloud. A line from Ghalib: the drop of water finds the river and is lost. Wah, wah.
practices.why: The sher is the basic unit of the ghazal, a self-contained couplet. Writing one is a rewarding way to compress a feeling.
variations: Share it with a friend.
Write one in the style of Ghalib.
Copy it in your best hand.

practices.name: A charbagh picnic
practices.instructions: Take a cloth, cushions, fruit, sweets, tea and a book of poems to a park or garden, and spread out in the Mughal style. Choose a spot near water or a tree. Read aloud, play a game, watch the light. Babur picnicked in his gardens and wrote poems. Eat mangoes if they are in season. Leave the place cleaner than you found it.
practices.why: The Mughal gardens were built for pleasure, picnics and poetry. A day in one, or in any green place, recreates their spirit.
variations: Bring a friend and a poem.
Bring a sketchbook.
Pick a spot with a view.

practices.name: A mushaira
practices.instructions: Hold a mushaira, a poetry gathering. Invite friends to bring a poem each, their own or a favourite, and read in turn with a lamp passed along. The audience calls wah or irshad (say it again) when a line pleases them. Serve tea and sweets. Poems can be in any language. Keep it warm, funny and generous.
practices.why: The mushaira is the great Urdu poetry gathering, still held in India and Pakistan. The audience takes part, calling out praise and asking for repeats.
variations: Ask each guest to read in their mother tongue.
Pass a candle for the reader.
End with a collective verse.

immersePlan.name: Read a stretch of the Baburnama
immersePlan.text: Read a section of Babur’s memoirs, perhaps his description of Kabul’s gardens or Hindustan’s plants and animals. Note his honesty.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of The Last Mughal
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of William Dalrymple’s story of Delhi in 1857 and the last emperor, a poet. Notice the city.

immersePlan.name: Read Ghalib
immersePlan.text: Read a handful of Mirza Ghalib’s ghazals and a letter in translation. Choose a couplet to learn.

immersePlan.name: Watch part of Mughal-e-Azam
immersePlan.text: Watch the first hour of K. Asif’s 1960 epic of Prince Salim and Anarkali, famous for its Sheesh Mahal song. Feel the splendour.

immersePlan.name: Watch Jodhaa Akbar
immersePlan.text: Watch Ashutosh Gowariker’s 2008 film of the marriage of Akbar and the Rajput princess Jodhaa. Notice the dialogue about tolerance.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of Mirza Ghalib
immersePlan.text: Watch an episode of Gulzar’s 1988 television series on the poet, with Naseeruddin Shah. Hear the ghazals.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Raga Darbari Kanada
immersePlan.text: Play Ustad Amir Khan or another master in the majestic night raga attributed to Tansen. Let it unfold slowly.

immersePlan.name: Listen to dhrupad
immersePlan.text: Play the oldest living form of Hindustani vocal music, sung by the Dagar family. Listen for the deep, sustained notes.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Begum Akhtar sing Ghalib
immersePlan.text: Play a ghazal of Ghalib sung by Begum Akhtar. Follow the translation of a couplet.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Taj Mahal
immersePlan.text: Look at the white marble tomb built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Notice the symmetry and the inlay.

immersePlan.name: Look at Mansur’s natural history studies
immersePlan.text: Look at Ustad Mansur’s paintings of a zebra, a turkey and a Himalayan monal. Notice how closely he looked.

immersePlan.name: Look at Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings
immersePlan.text: Look at Bichitr’s allegorical painting in which Jahangir hands a book to a humble sheikh instead of to the kings behind him. Count the figures.

immersePlan.name: Cook biryani
immersePlan.text: Layer spiced rice and meat or vegetables, seal the pot with dough and cook slowly on a low flame. Open it at the table.

immersePlan.name: Cook khichdi
immersePlan.text: Cook rice and lentils soft with ghee and cumin. It was Akbar’s favourite, and Birbal’s famous joke is about it.

immersePlan.name: Eat a ripe mango
immersePlan.text: Eat a ripe mango slowly, hands and all, in its season. Babur and Jahangir praised it as the best fruit of Hindustan.

immersePlan.name: Make rose sherbet
immersePlan.text: Stir rose syrup into cold water with lemon and a few basil seeds. Serve it in a tall glass.

immersePlan.name: Drink water from a clay jar
immersePlan.text: Drink cool water from a clay pot, which keeps it fresh. Akbar called the Ganges water the water of immortality and carried it everywhere; choose any clean water.

immersePlan.name: Make lassi
immersePlan.text: Churn yogurt with water and sugar or salt until frothy. Pour a glass and sit in the shade.

immersePlan.name: Weigh yourself in gifts
immersePlan.text: Calculate your weight, and give away that weight in food, clothes or goods, as the emperor did on his birthday. Give an amount symbolic of it to a charity.

immersePlan.name: Give a gift of honour
immersePlan.text: Give someone a gift of honour, a scarf, a flower or a book, to mark their service or friendship. Present it with both hands.

immersePlan.name: Practise mushaira manners
immersePlan.text: Listen to a poem and call wah or irshad after the lines you love. Practise appreciation aloud.

immersePlan.name: Play chaupar
immersePlan.text: Play the Mughal race game on a cross-shaped cloth board with dice or cowries. Play at least two games.

immersePlan.name: Play ganjifa
immersePlan.text: Play with painted round cards, or an ordinary pack. Make a trick-taking game with a friend.

immersePlan.name: Play a polo-style game
immersePlan.text: Chaugan was Persian polo, which Akbar played at night with glowing balls. Play a hockey or hobby-horse game with a stick and ball in a safe space.

immersePlan.name: Mark Nauroz
immersePlan.text: Nauroz, around 21 March, was celebrated at the Mughal court with gardens and gifts. Wish someone a happy new year.

immersePlan.name: Look up Fatehpur Sikri
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of Akbar’s red sandstone city near Agra, abandoned after fifteen years. Find the House of Worship.

immersePlan.name: Look up Humayun’s Tomb
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the 1560s garden-tomb in Delhi, precursor of the Taj Mahal. Notice the four-part garden.

immersePlan.name: Practise sulh-i kull
immersePlan.text: Sulh-i kull is peace with all. Wish peace to three people today, including one you disagree with.

immersePlan.name: Practise adab
immersePlan.text: Adab is courtesy and refinement. Use a formal courteous greeting once today.

immersePlan.name: Practise charbagh
immersePlan.text: A charbagh is a four-part garden. Sketch the plan of one, with four quarters round a central pool.

rules.why: Quarrel with no one over their beliefs. Protect everyone under your roof alike.
Do not hide from those who depend on you. Give them a regular time and listen.
Observe one thing each day as if you would have to paint it.
No flattering account. Set down what happened.
Greet, thank and give way with grace. Courtesy costs nothing and governs everything.
Whatever you build, cook, write or plant, finish it well. Leave a garden behind you.

read.title: The Baburnama: Memoirs of Babur, Prince and Emperor
read.creator: Babur, trans. Wheeler M. Thackston
read.why: One of the great autobiographies. A homesick prince from Central Asia loses a kingdom, wins another and writes down everything from his defeats to the taste of mangoes.

read.title: The Empire of the Great Mughals
read.creator: Annemarie Schimmel
read.why: A scholar’s loving survey of court life: women, religion, books, jewels, food, gardens and painting.

read.title: The Great Moghuls
read.creator: Bamber Gascoigne
read.why: The six great emperors from Babur to Aurangzeb, told as a family story. Still the most readable introduction.

read.title: The Last Mughal
read.creator: William Dalrymple
read.why: Delhi in 1857: the poet-emperor Zafar, the uprising and the destruction of a civilisation, drawn from thousands of unread Urdu and Persian papers.

read.title: The Jahangirnama
read.creator: Jahangir, trans. Wheeler M. Thackston
read.why: The memoirs of an emperor who was more interested in birds, meteorites and painting than in war.

read.title: Ghalib: Selected Poems and Letters
read.creator: Mirza Ghalib, trans. Frances W. Pritchett and Owen T. A. Cornwall
read.why: The greatest Urdu poet, who watched the Mughal world end. His letters are as good as his verse.

watch.title: Mughal-e-Azam
watch.creator: K. Asif
watch.why: Prince Salim loves a court dancer and defies his father Akbar. The grandest of all Hindi films, sixteen years in the making, with a famous song filmed in a hall of mirrors.

watch.title: Jodhaa Akbar
watch.creator: Ashutosh Gowariker
watch.why: The young Akbar and his Rajput wife learn to respect each other’s faith. Romantic and inventive with the facts, and good on the idea of peace with all.

watch.title: The Great Moghuls
watch.creator: Channel 4; presented by Bamber Gascoigne
watch.why: Six documentary films shot in the palaces, tombs and gardens.

watch.title: Mirza Ghalib
watch.creator: Gulzar
watch.why: A television series on the poet’s life in the last days of Mughal Delhi, with the ghazals sung by Jagjit Singh.

listen.title: Dhrupad
listen.creator: The Dagar family, or the Gundecha Brothers
listen.why: The oldest surviving form of North Indian classical singing, slow and austere, as it was sung at Akbar’s court.

listen.title: Raga Darbari Kanada
listen.creator: Ustad Amir Khan, or Pandit Bhimsen Joshi
listen.why: The raga of the court, grave and deep, for late at night.

listen.title: Ghazals of Ghalib
listen.creator: Begum Akhtar
listen.why: The queen of the ghazal sings the last great poet of Mughal Delhi.

listen.title: Qawwali at Nizamuddin
listen.creator: The hereditary qawwals of the shrine in Delhi
listen.why: Devotional songs in the form created by Amir Khusrau, sung every Thursday evening at the tomb of the saint the Mughals revered.

art.title: The Taj Mahal
art.creator: Built for Shah Jahan; attributed to Ustad Ahmad Lahori
art.why: The tomb of Mumtaz Mahal at Agra, in white marble inlaid with flowers and scripture, set at the end of a fourfold garden and not at its centre.

art.title: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings
art.creator: Bichitr
art.why: The emperor on an hourglass throne hands a book to a holy man and ignores the Ottoman sultan and King James of England. In the Freer Gallery, Washington.

art.title: Natural history studies
art.creator: Ustad Mansur
art.why: A zebra, a turkey cock, a chameleon, Kashmiri flowers and one of the few paintings of a dodo from life. Jahangir titled him Wonder of the Age.

art.title: The Padshahnama
art.creator: Court painters of Shah Jahan
art.why: The illustrated chronicle of the reign: weddings, sieges and darbars in which every face is a portrait. In the Royal Collection at Windsor.

eat.title: Biryani
eat.creator: Rice and spiced meat cooked together in a sealed pot
eat.why: The festive dish of the Mughal world, descended from Persian pilaf and made its own by every Indian city.

eat.title: Khichdi
eat.creator: Rice and lentils cooked soft with ghee
eat.why: Abu’l-Fazl gives the recipe from Akbar’s kitchen. Jahangir was so pleased with a Gujarati version that he ordered it served on his meatless days.

eat.title: Kebabs
eat.creator: Minced or cubed meat grilled on skewers
eat.why: The imperial kitchen list in the Ain-i Akbari names several kinds.

eat.title: Mangoes
eat.creator: Eaten ripe, in season
eat.why: Babur thought them overrated. His descendants were devoted: Akbar planted an orchard of a hundred thousand trees.

drink.title: Sherbet
drink.creator: Rose, pomegranate or falsa berries in sweetened water, chilled
drink.why: Ice was brought from the mountains by relays of boats and runners to cool the court’s drinks.

drink.title: Water from the Ganges
drink.creator: Carried in sealed jars
drink.why: Akbar called it the water of immortality and drank nothing else, at home or on campaign.

drink.title: Lassi
drink.creator: Churned yoghurt, salted or sweet
drink.why: The drink of the plains, cooling in the heat.

customs.title: The weighing of the emperor
customs.creator: Twice a year, on his birthdays
customs.why: He sat in one pan of a great golden scale and was weighed against gold, silver, grain and cloth, which were then given to the poor. The custom was taken from Hindu kings.

customs.title: Robes of honour
customs.creator: Khilat
customs.why: Favour was shown by the gift of clothing, and ambassadors, poets and governors were robed in open court.

customs.title: Paan at parting
customs.creator: A folded leaf from the host’s hand
customs.why: The sign that an audience or a meal is over, and that the guest leaves in favour.

customs.title: The manners of the mushaira
customs.creator: Appreciation aloud
customs.why: A good couplet is met with cries of praise and a request to hear it again. A poet acknowledges it by raising a hand to the forehead.

games.title: Chaupar
games.creator: Board game · India
games.why: A race game on a cross-shaped cloth, close to pachisi. Akbar is said to have played it at Fatehpur Sikri on a courtyard marked out in stone, with people as the pieces.

games.title: Ganjifa
games.creator: Card game · Persia and India
games.why: Round hand-painted cards in eight or more suits. Babur sent a pack to a friend, and Akbar devised his own version.

games.title: Shatranj
games.creator: Chess · India and Persia
games.why: Played throughout the court in its older form, with an elephant in place of the bishop and a minister in place of the queen.

games.title: Chaugan
games.creator: Polo · Persia and Central Asia
games.why: Akbar played it by night with a ball of smouldering wood, and required his nobles to play so that he could judge their character.

festivals.title: Nauroz
festivals.creator: Around 21 March
festivals.why: The Persian new year at the spring equinox. The court kept it for nineteen days with gifts, a palace bazaar and the weighing of the emperor.

festivals.title: Diwali and Holi at court
festivals.creator: Autumn and spring, by the Hindu calendar
festivals.why: Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan all took part. The Red Fort was lit with lamps, and paintings show emperors playing with colour.

festivals.title: Phool Walon Ki Sair
festivals.creator: September or October, in Mehrauli, Delhi
festivals.why: The procession of the flower sellers, begun under the Mughals in 1812. Floral fans are offered at both a Sufi shrine and a Hindu temple.

festivals.title: Eid
festivals.creator: At the end of Ramadan, by the lunar calendar
festivals.why: The emperor rode in procession to the great mosque and gave robes and alms.

places.title: The Taj Mahal and Agra Fort
places.creator: Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
places.why: Go to the Taj at sunrise. From the fort across the bend of the river you can stand where Shah Jahan, deposed by his son, spent his last years looking at it.

places.title: Fatehpur Sikri
places.creator: Near Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
places.why: Akbar’s red sandstone capital, built in the 1570s and left after fourteen years. The courts, the great gate and the white tomb of the saint are almost intact.

places.title: Humayun’s Tomb
places.creator: Nizamuddin, New Delhi, India
places.why: The first great garden tomb, built by his widow in the 1560s, and the model for the Taj. The restored garden and the nursery park beside it are a pleasure to walk.

places.title: The Red Fort
places.creator: Old Delhi, India
places.why: Shah Jahan’s palace of 1648. The marble halls with the paradise inscription survive among later barracks. The old city he founded lies at its gate.

places.title: Lahore Fort and the Shalimar Gardens
places.creator: Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
places.why: A second capital. The fort has a hall of mirrors and a wall of tile pictures, and the terraced gardens of 1641 still run with water on special days.

places.title: The Garden of Babur
places.creator: Kabul, Afghanistan
places.why: The hillside garden he laid out and asked to be buried in, under the open sky. Restored in the 2000s. Check current travel advice.

ethics.title: Peace with all
ethics.text: No community is to be favoured or persecuted. Akbar abolished the tax on non-Muslims and forbade forced conversion.
ethics.practice: Treat someone whose beliefs you dislike with exact fairness today.

ethics.title: Justice
ethics.text: The emperor’s first duty was to be reachable by the wronged.
ethics.practice: Hear out someone who has a grievance against you, to the end.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: A ruler was judged by his open hand. Twice a year the emperor’s own weight in gold went to the poor.
ethics.practice: Give away something of real value.

ethics.title: Courtesy
ethics.text: Adab governs how people of unequal power can live together without humiliation.
ethics.practice: Greet the person of lowest rank in the room first.

ethics.title: Truthfulness
ethics.text: Babur’s memoirs record his own defeats, fears and follies.
ethics.practice: Tell one story today in which you do not come out well.

ethics.title: Stewardship of beauty
ethics.text: Gardens, books and buildings were made to outlast their makers.
ethics.practice: Mend or tend one beautiful thing you did not make.

philosophy.title: Sulh-i kull
philosophy.text: Truth is too large for one religion. A just ruler therefore stands above all of them and keeps the peace among them. It was a political idea as much as a spiritual one.
philosophy.practice: Where do you insist others share your view before you will work with them?

philosophy.title: The ruler as light
philosophy.text: Abu’l-Fazl taught that kingship is a ray from God, given so that the king may care for all people as a father. It raised the emperor above the clergy.
philosophy.practice: What gives anyone the right to rule, in your view?

philosophy.title: Reason over tradition
philosophy.text: Akbar’s circle held that inherited belief must answer to reason. He tested claims by experiment, once raising infants in silence to find the natural language.
philosophy.practice: Which of your beliefs have you only inherited?

philosophy.title: The world as a bridge
philosophy.text: The gateway at Fatehpur Sikri tells the visitor to cross the world and build no house on it. The city behind it was abandoned within a generation.
philosophy.practice: What are you building as if it would last?

philosophy.title: Looking as knowledge
philosophy.text: Jahangir trusted his own eyes over the books. To paint a thing exactly was to know it.
philosophy.practice: What do you think you know but have never examined?

philosophy.title: The garden as paradise
philosophy.text: A garden is order, water and shade made in a harsh land: an image of the next world and a claim on this one.
philosophy.practice: What small paradise can you make where you are?

philosophy.title: The meeting of two seas
philosophy.text: Prince Dara Shikoh translated the Upanishads into Persian and wrote that Hindu and Muslim mystics had found the same ocean. His brother had him killed for it.
philosophy.practice: What two traditions meet in you?

philosophy.title: Splendour and its cost
philosophy.text: The Taj was paid for by the taxes of peasants, and the empire’s wars emptied its treasury. Beauty and burden came together.
philosophy.practice: Who pays for the beautiful things you enjoy?

intro: The Mughal Empire was founded in 1526 by a prince from Central Asia named Babur. He was descended from Timur on his father’s side and Chinggis Khan on his mother’s, and he had spent his youth winning and losing the city of Samarkand. Driven from his homeland, he took Kabul, and from there led a small army with cannon into the plains of northern India and defeated the Sultan of Delhi. He found the country hot, dusty and without good melons, and he stayed. He also wrote one of the most candid memoirs any ruler has left.

His grandson Akbar, who came to the throne at thirteen in 1556 and reigned for forty-nine years, made the conquest into an empire. He was a formidable soldier and could not read, probably because of what we would now call dyslexia, and he had books read to him every day. He understood that a Muslim dynasty ruling a largely Hindu population could not last by force. He married Rajput princesses and made their fathers and brothers his generals. He abolished the tax on non-Muslims, forbade forced conversion, had the Hindu epics translated into Persian, and invited scholars of every religion to debate in his presence. His principle was sulh-i kull, peace with all.

Under Akbar and his successors Jahangir and Shah Jahan, the empire was among the richest states on earth, with perhaps a hundred million people and a quarter of the world’s manufacturing. Its nobility was drawn from Iran, Central Asia, Afghanistan and India and ranked by a single system of numbered grades. Its court language was Persian. Its culture was a deliberate blend. Painters trained in the Persian manner learned from Indian colourists and European prints, and produced a school of miniature painting of extraordinary delicacy. Architects joined the Persian dome and garden to Indian stone carving, and built Fatehpur Sikri, the Red Forts of Agra and Delhi and, for Shah Jahan’s wife, the Taj Mahal. Musicians, cooks, perfumers and poets worked in the same spirit.

The sixth emperor, Aurangzeb, was an austere and tireless man who seized the throne from his father in 1658 and killed his brother Dara Shikoh, the heir who had tried to reconcile Hindu and Muslim thought. He extended the empire to its greatest size and exhausted it in twenty-six years of war in the south. He reimposed the tax on non-Muslims and is remembered very differently by different communities. After his death in 1707 the provinces broke away. A Persian invader carried off the Peacock Throne in 1739, and the British East India Company gradually became the real power.

The emperors remained in the Red Fort as pensioners, and Delhi enjoyed a last flowering of Urdu poetry. In 1857 rebel soldiers proclaimed the aged poet-emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader. The British retook the city, shot his sons and exiled him to Rangoon, where he died.

The Mughals left the subcontinent much of what the world thinks of as Indian: its best-known building, its court cuisine, its classical music in the north, the Urdu language, and an ideal of civility shared across faiths. This Onda draws on the court at its best: the ruler visible at sunrise, the honest diary, the house of dialogue, the garden and the evening of verse.
guide.origin: The Ferghana valley and Kabul, then the plains of northern India: Agra, Delhi and Lahore
guide.era: Babur won Delhi in 1526. The last emperor was exiled by the British in 1858

figures.name: Babur
figures.bio: Founder of the dynasty. Soldier, gardener, poet and diarist, who missed the mountains of his youth all his life.

figures.name: Gulbadan Begum
figures.bio: Babur’s daughter. At her nephew Akbar’s request she wrote a memoir of her father and brother, the only surviving history of the period by a woman of the court.

figures.name: Humayun
figures.bio: The second emperor, who lost the kingdom, spent fifteen years in exile in Persia, won it back and died within a year, falling on his library stairs.

figures.name: Akbar
figures.bio: The third emperor and the true architect of the empire. Restless, curious, physically fearless and uninterested in doctrine.

figures.name: Abu'l-Fazl
figures.bio: Akbar’s friend, minister and historian. His Akbarnama and its appendix, the Ain-i Akbari, describe the empire down to the price of mangoes.

figures.name: Tansen
figures.bio: The foremost singer of the age, one of the nine jewels of Akbar’s court. Legends say his ragas could bring rain and light lamps.

figures.name: Jahangir
figures.bio: The fourth emperor: naturalist, connoisseur and drinker, who left much of the governing to his wife.

figures.name: Nur Jahan
figures.bio: Born on the road as her Persian parents fled to India. Jahangir’s twentieth wife and in effect co-ruler: coins were struck in her name, and she was a crack shot.

figures.name: Shah Jahan
figures.bio: The fifth emperor, the great builder. He spent his last eight years confined in Agra Fort.

figures.name: Jahanara Begum
figures.bio: Shah Jahan’s eldest daughter, first lady of the court after her mother’s death, a Sufi writer, and the designer of the main street of Delhi.

figures.name: Dara Shikoh
figures.bio: The heir apparent, a mystic and scholar who translated fifty Upanishads into Persian. Defeated and executed by his younger brother.

figures.name: Aurangzeb
figures.bio: The sixth emperor, who ruled for forty-nine years. Pious, frugal and unbending, he sewed caps to pay for his own tomb.

figures.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar
figures.bio: The last emperor, a calligrapher and poet with no power beyond his palace walls.

history.detail: Babur’s twelve thousand men, with field guns and matchlocks, defeat the far larger army of the Sultan of Delhi.
Humayun is driven out by the Afghan ruler Sher Shah, whose roads and coinage the Mughals later adopt. He returns with Persian help.
The thirteen-year-old is enthroned in a garden in Punjab. His regent wins a second battle at Panipat to secure the throne.
Akbar marries a princess of Amber and takes her family into his service. He abolishes the pilgrim tax and the poll tax on non-Muslims.
A new capital is built beside the hermitage of a Sufi saint. The House of Worship opens there in 1575.
Queen Elizabeth charters a company of London merchants to trade with the East. Its envoy reaches Jahangir’s court in 1615.
Jahangir marries the widow Mihr un-Nisa. Her family dominates the court for a generation.
Mumtaz Mahal dies bearing her fourteenth child. Some twenty thousand workers spend two decades on her tomb.
The court moves to a new walled city at Delhi, with the Red Fort and the largest mosque in India.
Aurangzeb defeats his brothers, imprisons his father and has Dara Shikoh paraded in rags and put to death.
Aurangzeb leaves the north for the last time to fight the southern sultanates and the Marathas. He dies in camp at eighty-eight.
The ruler of Persia sacks Delhi, kills many thousands and takes away the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.
After victories in Bengal the British become the main power in India. In 1803 they take Delhi and the emperor under their protection.
The great uprising makes Zafar its figurehead. After the fall of Delhi he is tried, exiled to Burma, and the dynasty is declared extinct.

concepts.detail: The doctrine that the emperor is the impartial protector of all faiths. It was the ideological core of Akbar’s state and was kept, with lapses, by his son and grandson.
Every officer held a numbered rank that set his salary and military obligation. Ranks were not hereditary, so the nobility depended on the emperor.
Under Akbar’s Hindu finance minister, Todar Mal, fields were surveyed and tax fixed on average yields. It was the foundation of the empire’s wealth.
A small circle of disciples formed around Akbar in 1582, devoted to the emperor and to the worship of God through light. It had no scripture or clergy and died with him.
Akbar had the Mahabharata, the Ramayana and other works translated and illustrated so that his nobles might understand their Hindu subjects.
The walled, four-part garden as the setting for court life and as a tomb. Inscriptions compare them outright to the gardens promised in scripture.
A painting might have one master for the design, another for the colouring and a third for the faces. More than a hundred painters worked for Akbar.
Persian was the tongue of government and letters from Istanbul to Bengal. From its meeting with the speech of Delhi came Urdu.
The daily appearance at the window, which let the people see their ruler as a Hindu deity is seen. Aurangzeb ended it as un-Islamic.

facts.text: The Taj Mahal changes colour through the day, from pink at dawn to white at noon and gold at dusk.
Akbar’s library held some twenty-four thousand volumes, though he could not read them himself.
The Peacock Throne took seven years to make and cost twice as much as the Taj Mahal.
The word mogul, for a powerful person, comes from the Persian for Mongol, a name the dynasty did not use for itself.
Jahangir had the death of a famous courtier painted from life, so that the effects of opium and drink might be recorded.
Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal lie in plain graves in a crypt below the Taj. The decorated tombs above are empty.

sensitivity.note: The Mughal past is argued over in South Asia today, sometimes bitterly. This Onda draws on the court’s ideals of peace among faiths, close observation and refinement. It reports the conquests and the intolerance as well, and takes no side in present-day politics.
requiredCaveats: The empire was founded and enlarged by war. Temples were destroyed at various times, and two Sikh Gurus were executed on the orders of Mughal emperors.
Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs remember particular emperors, Aurangzeb above all, in sharply different ways. Read historians from more than one community.
The splendour of the court rested on heavy taxation of the peasantry.
The culture described here belongs to the living peoples of India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. Enjoy it as a guest.
